On 1 January 1962 Western Samoa became independent from New Zealand, the first Pacific island country to do so in the 20th century. It shortened its name to Samoa in 1997.

The Mau had kept up the demand for decades, and after the Second World War the United Nations pressed New Zealand to prepare self-rule. The constitution blended Samoan custom with parliament: for decades only matai, the family chiefs, could stand or vote.

Universal suffrage came only in 1991. Samoa kept close ties with New Zealand, and Samoans became one of its largest Pacific communities. Its example was soon followed by Fiji, Tonga and others.
